What it does?

\n

This tool extracts data (in fastq format) from the Short Read Archive (SRA) at the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). It is based on the fasterq-dump utility of the SRA Toolkit. The following applies:

\n
\n
    \n

  • if data is paired-ended (or mate-pair) the tool will generate a collection of file pairs, in which each element will be a pair of fastq files containing forward and reverse mates.

    \n
    • \n

  • if data is single ended, each element of the collection will be a single fastq dataset.

    \n
    \n

    How to use it?

    \n
    \n
    • \n
\n
\n

There are three ways in which you can download data:

\n
\n
    \n
  1. Plain text input of accession number(s)
    2. \n
  2. Providing a list of accessions from file
    3. \n
  3. Extracting data from an already uploaded SRA dataset
    4. \n
\n
\n

Below we discuss each in detail.

\n
\n

Purpose

\n

pysradb allows to retrieve metadata from BioProject ID or search run accession numbers and metadata, from SRA and ENA based on multiple criteria:

\n
    \n
  • BioProject ID
    • \n
  • Database: SRA or ENA
    • \n
  • Query keywords
    • \n
  • Accession number: a relevant study/experiment/sample/run accession number
    • \n
  • Organism: scientific name of the sample organism
    • \n
  • Library layout: paired or single-end reads
    • \n
  • Sample size: rounded to the nearest megabase
    • \n
  • Publication date
    • \n
  • Sequencing platform: Illumina, Nanopore or PacBio
    • \n
  • Library selection: method used to select and/or enrich the material being sequenced
    • \n
  • Library source: Type of source material that is being sequenced
    • \n
  • Library preparation strategy: sequencing technique intended for the library
    • \n
\n
\n

Outputs

\n

pysradb generates three different output types:

\n
    \n
  • Raw metadata file
    • \n
  • Statistics for the search query
    • \n
  • Graphs to illustrate the search results
    • \n
\n
\n

Sequencing instruments

\n

Comparisons between HiSeq instruments

\n

HiSeq 3000/4000 provides some improvements with respect the previous model HiSeq 2500:

\n
    \n
  • HiSeq 3000/4000 genere up to 1.5 Tb and 5 Tb reads per run.
    • \n
  • HiSeq 3000/4000 use patterned flow cell technology originally developed for HiSeq X platforms.
    • \n
  • HiSeq 3000/4000 run 3 times faster and yield 65% more reads per lane.
    • \n
  • HiSeq 3000/4000 patterned flow cells contain billions of nanowells at fixed, known positions on the flow cell. The structured organization enables clustering at higher densities compared to non-pattern HiSeq designs.
    • \n
\n

However, the HiSeq 3000/4000 also have some also some limitations with respect to HiSeq 2500:

\n
    \n
  • HiSeq 3000/4000 are not recommended for low complexity sequencing. Applications such as non-unique amplicons, 16S, are currently not recommended.
    • \n
  • Libraries with low complexity within the first 25 bases of a read are not expected to produce high quality data.
    • \n
  • Library size restrictions. Libraries that are too long can result in polyclonal clusters that span more than 1 well, these will not pass filter. Smaller libraries will preferentially amplify with Illumina's new kinetic exclusion amplification so tight library distributions ranging from 300-500 bp are recommended.
    • \n
  • Very low tolerance for adapter dimers. Even as little as 1% adapter dimer can take up ~6% of sequencing reads, 10% contamination will take up 84% of reads. Illumina recommends you keep adapter contamination below 0.5% of your entire library.
    • \n
  • Higher duplication rates as compared to HiSeq 2500.
    • \n
  • Low quality read 2 (entire HiSeq 3000 install base is affected).
    • \n
\n

HiSeq 3000/4000 support DNA-seq, RNA-seq , ChIP-Seq, mate-pair, small RNA and exome library preparation. Any library preparation where there is enough sequence diversity is currently supported. Amplicon, 16S and applications with low sequencing diversity are currently not supported on the HiSeq 3000 / 4000.

\n

HiSeq 2500 is considered the most reliable model according to different sources.

\n

What type of read quality is expected from the HiSeq 3000/4000 ?

\n
    \n
  • 2 x 50bp \u226585% bases > Q30
    • \n
  • 2 x 75bp \u226580% bases > Q30
    • \n
  • 2 x 150bp \u226575% of bases >Q30
    • \n
\n

What is the difference between MiSeq and HiSeq?

\n

HiSeq and MiSeq platforms are among the most widely used platform to study microbial communities. But the two platforms differ in the length and amount of reads.\nMiSeq can run 600 cycles to produce 200 million 300 bp reads, on the other hand, HiSeq 2500 can run 500 cycles to produce 120 million 250 bp.

\n

What are the differences between HiSeq and NovaSeq?

\n

The Illumina NovaSeq provides a massive upgrade in sequencing throughput compared to the HiSeq 4000. There are more stringent library requirements and requires a\nlarger sample size. Due to the vast amount of data produced by the NovaSeq and the known issue of index swapping, unique dual-indexed libraries are required.

\n

What are the characteristics of HiSeq X instruments?

\n
    \n
  • HiSeq X is recommended for whole genome sequencing only (including whole bisulfite sequencing). This means that it is not adequate for RNA-seq, exome, ChIP-seq or small RNA-seq applications.
    • \n
  • Plant and animal samples can be sequenced on the HiSeq X.
    • \n
  • Expect coverate is over 30x or approximately 375 million reads per lane by loading one sample per lane.
    • \n
  • Hiseq X Ten generates utilize 2x150 base pair read configurations and has slightly better GC coverage than the HiSeq 2500.
    • \n
\n

What are the differences between MiSeq and Nextseq?

\n

The NextSeq Series of systems delivers the power of high-throughput sequencing with the simplicity of a desktop sequencer. NextSeq instruments represent an improvement when compared with Miseq, despite generating sorter reads (150bp, compared to MiSeq 250bp). NextSeq is recommended in\nthe following applications & methods:

\n
    \n
  • Exome & large panel sequencing (enrichment-based)
    • \n
  • Single-cell profiling (scRNA-Seq, scDNA-Seq, oligo tagging assays)
    • \n
  • Transcriptome sequencing (total RNA-Seq, mRNA-Seq, gene expression profiling)
    • \n
  • Methylation sequencing
    • \n
  • Metagenomic profiling (shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics)
    • \n
  • Cell-free sequencing & liquid biopsy analysis
    • \n
\n

Regarding the maximum number of reads per ran, MiSeq can generate 25 million, vs 400 million generated by the Nextseq 550 instrument. MiSeq recommended for sequencing samples of low diversity.

\n

What are the differences between HiSeq and NextSeq?

\n

The main technical difference between HiSeq and NextSeq will be the number of dyes each machines use. HiSeq uses traditional color coding with four different dyes, while NextSeq uses two dyes. This does not give any practical differences in terms of the data quality, but the trend in illumina sequencers are more into the direction of reducing the number of dyes.

\n

What is the difference between Nextseq and NovaSeq?

\n

The NovaSeq 6000 system offers deep and broad coverage and is recommended for large whole-genome sequencing (human, plant, animal) projects. It generates 250 bp reads,\nwith 20 billion maximum reads per run. NovaSeq 6000 instruments have not application based restrictions.

\n

Illumina maximum read-length summary

\n
    \n
  • MiSeq: between 300 and 600 bp
    • \n
  • NextSeq: 300 bp
    • \n
  • HiSeq 2500: between 250 and 500 bp (depending of the sofware)
    • \n
  • HiSeq 4000: 150 bp
    • \n
  • HiSeq X: 150 bp
    • \n
\n

Nanopore models - single-molecule ultra-long-read sequencing

\n

/usr/bin/bash -lc "set -euo pipefail
req_meta='bioproject run_accession study_accession experiment_accession sample_accession biosample organism_taxid organism_name library_strategy library_source library_selection library_layout instrument_model run_total_spots run_total_bases'
req_manifest='bioproject run_accession library_layout forward_path reverse_path'
for acc in PRJNA1354216 PRJNA1339024; do
  f=\"final_answer/metadata/"'$acc.tsv"
  [ -f "$f" ]
  awk -F '"'\\t' -v acc=\""'$acc" -v req="$req_meta" '"'
    NR==1 { for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) col["'$i]=i; n=split(req,a," "); for(i=1;i<=n;i++) if(!(a[i] in col)){print "missing metadata column",a[i] > "/dev/stderr"; exit 2} next }
    { if($col["bioproject"]!=acc){print "wrong bioproject",NR > "/dev/stderr"; exit 3}; if($col["run_accession"]==""){print "empty run",NR > "/dev/stderr"; exit 4}; if(seen[$col["run_accession"]]++){print "duplicate run",$col["run_accession"] > "/dev/stderr"; exit 5}; rows++ }
    END { if(rows<1){print "no metadata rows" > "/dev/stderr"; exit 6}; print acc,"metadata_rows",rows,"columns",NF }
  '"' \""'$f"
done
awk -F '"'\\t' -v req=\""'$req_manifest" '"'
  NR==1 { for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) col["'$i]=i; n=split(req,a," "); for(i=1;i<=n;i++) if(!(a[i] in col)){print "missing manifest column",a[i] > "/dev/stderr"; exit 2}; next }
  { if(seen[$col["run_accession"]]++){print "duplicate manifest run",$col["run_accession"] > "/dev/stderr"; exit 3}; if($col["library_layout"]!="SINGLE" && $col["library_layout"]!="PAIRED"){print "bad layout",NR > "/dev/stderr"; exit 4}; if($col["forward_path"]=="" || $col["forward_path"] ~ /''^'"\\// || "'$col["reverse_path"] ~ /''^'"\\//){print \"bad path\",NR > \"/dev/stderr\"; exit 5}; if("'$col["library_layout"]=="SINGLE" && $col["reverse_path"]!=""){print "single has reverse",NR > "/dev/stderr"; exit 6}; if($col["library_layout"]=="PAIRED" && $col["reverse_path"]==""){print "paired lacks reverse",NR > "/dev/stderr"; exit 7}; runs[$col["run_accession"]]=1; rows++ }
  END { if(rows!=20){print "manifest_rows",rows,"expected 20" > "/dev/stderr"; exit 8}; print "manifest_rows",rows }
'"' final_answer/run_manifest.tsv
# Compare run sets, including BioProject association.
awk -F '\\t' 'NR>1{print "'$1"'"\\t\""'$2}'"' final_answer/metadata/PRJNA1354216.tsv final_answer/metadata/PRJNA1339024.tsv | sort > /tmp/meta_runs.tsv
awk -F '\\t' 'NR>1{print "'$1"'"\\t\""'$2}'"' final_answer/run_manifest.tsv | sort > /tmp/manifest_runs.tsv
cmp /tmp/meta_runs.tsv /tmp/manifest_runs.tsv
# Verify every manifest path resolves under final_answer and exact expected read-file inventory.
while IFS="'$'"'\\t' read -r bp run layout fwd rev; do
  [ \""'$bp" != bioproject ] || continue
  case "$layout" in
    SINGLE) [ "$fwd" = "reads/${run}.fastq.gz" ]; [ -z "$rev" ];;
    PAIRED) [ "$fwd" = "reads/${run}_1.fastq.gz" ]; [ "$rev" = "reads/${run}_2.fastq.gz" ];;
  esac
  [ -f "final_answer/$fwd" ]
  if [ -n "$rev" ]; then [ -f "final_answer/$rev" ]; fi
done < final_answer/run_manifest.tsv
read_count=$(find final_answer/reads -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '"'*.fastq.gz' | wc -l)
[ \""'$read_count" -eq 32 ]
extra=$(find final_answer -type f ! -path '"'final_answer/metadata/PRJNA1354216.tsv' "'! -path '"'final_answer/metadata/PRJNA1339024.tsv' "'! -path '"'final_answer/run_manifest.tsv' "'! -path '"'final_answer/reads/*.fastq.gz' -print)
[ -z \""'$extra" ]
# Validate gzip members without rewriting any read data.
for f in final_answer/reads/*.fastq.gz; do gzip -t "$f"; done
printf '"'run_set_match=yes\\nread_files=%s\\ngzip_integrity=ok\\n' \""'$read_count"
'
